title: CHIME Telescope Catches 8-Billion-Year-Old Hydrogen Glow, Opening New Window on Dark Energy
excerpt: Using only its own observations, the Canadian radio telescope detected neutral hydrogen from the young universe — with Raman Research Institute scientists in the collaboration — validating a new technique to map cosmic expansion.
body:
• The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has detected the faint 21-centimetre radio glow of neutral hydrogen from about 8 billion light-years away — the first time the signal has been found using CHIME's own observations alone.
  • The result, published in The Astrophysical Journal on September 28, rests on 94 interference-free nights of data from 2019, selected from roughly 2,000 days of observations, and more than two years of analysis to separate the signal from background noise up to 10,000 times stronger.
  • Researchers from Bengaluru's Raman Research Institute participated in the CHIME collaboration behind the detection.
  • The measurement validates intensity mapping — charting hydrogen across vast cosmic volumes without cataloguing individual galaxies — as a faster, cheaper route to tracking how the universe expanded and testing theories of dark energy.

A Canadian radio telescope has picked up the faint radio glow of neutral hydrogen emitted when the universe was about five billion years old — a detection that could give cosmologists an entirely new way to map cosmic expansion and probe dark energy. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, or CHIME, reported the first standalone detection of the redshifted 21-centimetre hydrogen signal in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal on September 28.

Unlike earlier CHIME results, which cross-correlated its maps with galaxies identified by separate surveys, the team found the signal — the large-scale clustering of neutral hydrogen — in CHIME's data alone, at an average redshift of 1.16 and a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.4. Raman Research Institute scientists in Bengaluru were part of the collaboration.

Context & Background

Neutral hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe and the raw fuel for star formation. Its 21-centimetre emission line is a standard tracer of how matter is distributed — but from billions of light-years away, the signal is extraordinarily faint, easily drowned out by galactic synchrotron emission, human-made radio interference and even the telescope's own electronics.

India's radio astronomers know this challenge well. The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune has spent years pushing the same frontier: in 2022 a team using the GMRT, aided by a gravitational lens that magnified the signal 30-fold, captured 21-cm emission from 8.8 billion years ago — then the most distant such detection. CHIME's achievement is a different kind of milestone: a statistical, all-sky technique that works without such crutches.

CHIME itself is an unusual instrument: four cylindrical reflectors with no moving parts, watching the northern sky every day from the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory near Penticton, British Columbia. The team restricted the analysis to nighttime observations in a clean frequency band between 608.2 and 707.8 megahertz, corresponding to redshifts 1.34 to 1.01.

"We worked very hard to convince ourselves that this wasn't a false alarm. After all the tests, the signal remained. That gave us confidence we were seeing real hydrogen from the distant universe."

— Arnab Chakraborty, University of Toronto, CHIME collaboration

Impact & Analysis

The technique at the heart of the paper is intensity mapping: instead of laboriously cataloguing individual galaxies, the telescope records the collective hydrogen glow across enormous volumes of space at once. Because it surveys large scales quickly and at a fraction of the cost of optical galaxy surveys, it offers cosmologists a way to reconstruct the universe's expansion history across billions of years — and to test competing explanations for dark energy.

There are limits, and the authors are candid about them. To reach the detection, the team had to discard contaminated frequency modes — and those removed modes currently prevent a direct measurement of the universe's expansion rate. The collaboration is now developing techniques to recover those cosmological modes so the data can actually constrain dark energy. The longer-term prize is baryon acoustic oscillations — enormous patterns left by pressure waves in the hot early universe whose characteristic size serves as a cosmic standard ruler for reconstructing expansion history.

"By measuring how that hydrogen is distributed and clustered, CHIME gives us a new way to test our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve."

— Dr. Shabbir Shaikh, postdoctoral fellow, Arizona State University

Diaspora Angle

The result is a genuinely international piece of science, and Indian researchers are part of the story: the Raman Research Institute's participation places Bengaluru scientists inside a collaboration now defining a new observational method in cosmology. For a diaspora that takes pride in India's scientific institutions, CHIME's paper is another marker that Indian radio astronomy sits at the frontier of the field.

What's Next

The current measurement uses only a small fraction of CHIME's archive. The team has nearly seven years of observations banked and plans to mine them to push further back, toward the era when the universe was about three billion years old — and, eventually, to recover the modes that can constrain dark energy.
